question: What is rate limiting and why does an API need it?
answer_hinglish:
Rate limiting ka matlab hai: ek identity (IP, user, API key) ek time period mein kitni requests bhej sakti hai, uski upper limit. Limit cross hui toh hum request process nahi karte, seedha 429 Too Many Requests return karte hain.

Kyun chahiye? Paanch real reasons hain, aur is project ki `policies.json` mein har reason ke liye ek alag policy hai. Pehla, abuse aur flood protection -- `ip_global` har IP ko 300 requests per minute deta hai. Doosra, brute force rokna -- `login_bruteforce` login pe per IP 5 attempts per minute. Teesra, fair usage -- ek tenant poori capacity na kha jaye. Chautha, business model -- `user_plan` mein free plan 60/min, pro 600/min, enterprise 6000/min. Paanchva, downstream protection -- `reports_smooth` ek slow report service ko smooth traffic deta hai leaky bucket se.

Interview mein main yeh bolta hoon: rate limiter sirf security feature nahi hai, yeh capacity planning aur pricing ka bhi tool hai. Aur jab app multiple servers pe chalti hai tab limit "global" honi chahiye, isliye maine counters Redis mein rakhe aur har check ek atomic Lua script hai.
why_needed: Bina limit ke ek buggy client ya ek attacker poore system ki capacity kha sakta hai, aur baaki honest users ka latency badh jata hai ya service down ho jati hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek restaurant jiska ek hi kitchen hai: agar ek customer 500 orders ek saath de de toh baaki sab ka khana late. Rule banao: har table ek minute mein max 5 orders.
how_it_works: Har request pe identity nikalo, us identity ke counter/bucket ko check karo, limit ke andar ho toh allow aur counter update, warna 429 + Retry-After header. State shared store (Redis) mein hoti hai taaki saare app instances ek hi count dekhein.
in_this_project: `ratelimiter/policies.json` mein 5 policies aur 4 route groups (`default`, `search`, `login`, `reports`) hain. Har route `Depends(rate_limited("search"))` jaise dependency se apna group choose karta hai (`api/routes.py`).
advantages: Abuse aur brute force se protection
Pricing plans enforce ho jate hain
disadvantages: Har request pe ek extra Redis round-trip
Galat limits honest users ko block kar sakti hain
common_mistakes: Rate limiting ko sirf DDoS defence samajhna -- asli DDoS edge/CDN pe rokna padta hai
Limit sirf ek server ki memory mein rakhna jab app multiple servers pe hai
follow_up_questions: What happens when your rate limiter itself (Redis) is down?
Which algorithm did you use for login and why?
How do clients know when to retry?

question: When does this service return 429 and when does it return 503?
answer_hinglish:
429 Too Many Requests ka matlab: system healthy hai, lekin tumne apni limit cross kar di. 503 Service Unavailable ka matlab: hum decide hi nahi kar paaye kyunki dependency (Redis) available nahi hai, aur policy kehti hai ki aise case mein reject karo.

Is project mein `raise_if_denied` function yeh fark karta hai. Agar combined decision denied hai aur binding decision `degraded=False` hai toh `TooManyRequests` raise hota hai -- 429, `Retry-After` header (whole seconds, minimum 1) aur body mein `policy`, `algorithm`, `retry_after_ms`. Agar decision `degraded=True` hai, matlab Redis down tha aur policy `fail_mode=closed` thi (jaise `login_bruteforce`), toh `ServiceUnavailable` raise hota hai -- 503 + `Retry-After: 1`.

Ek aur 503 case hai: API key authentication. `ApiKeyStore.lookup` agar Redis error dekhe toh 503 deta hai, 500 nahi, kyunki hum valid aur forged key mein fark nahi kar sakte. Yeh `test_api_key_auth_fails_closed_with_503_not_500` prove karta hai.

Fark kyun important hai? Client ke liye 429 ka matlab "tum dheere chalo", 503 ka matlab "server ki problem hai, thodi der baad try karo". Monitoring mein bhi alag alert lagte hain.
why_needed: Client aur on-call engineer dono ko pata hona chahiye ki rejection unki galti hai (limit) ya system ki (dependency down).
real_world_analogy: Bank counter pe 429 matlab "aaj ki aapki withdrawal limit khatam"; 503 matlab "server down hai, abhi hum check hi nahi kar sakte, thodi der baad aao".
how_it_works: `check_one` Redis error pe `BackendUnavailable` pakad ke `Decision(degraded=True)` banata hai; allowed sirf tab jab `fail_mode` open hai. Phir `raise_if_denied` binding decision ko dekh ke 429 ya 503 choose karta hai. bpcommon ka error handler `AppError.headers` ko response pe laga deta hai.
in_this_project: `services/rate_limit_service.py::raise_if_denied` aur `test_failure_modes.py::test_http_fail_open_and_fail_closed_routes` -- Redis dead hone pe `/api/resource` 200 + `X-RateLimit-Status: degraded` deta hai aur `/api/login` 503 + `Retry-After: 1`.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: services/rate_limit_service.py
if d.degraded:  # fail-closed policy and backend is down
    raise ServiceUnavailable("Rate limiter unavailable; request rejected (fail-closed policy)",
                             details={"policy": d.policy}, headers={**headers, "Retry-After": "1"})
retry_s = max((d.retry_after_ms + 999) // 1000, 1)
headers["Retry-After"] = str(retry_s)
raise TooManyRequests(...)
advantages: Client sahi retry behaviour choose kar sakta hai
Alerts alag ho sakte hain (abuse vs outage)
disadvantages: Clients ko dono codes handle karne padte hain
common_mistakes: Redis down pe 500 return karna (unhandled exception)
Fail-closed case mein 429 dena -- client sochega usne limit cross ki
follow_up_questions: Why is Retry-After never 0?
What does the client see when a fail-open policy degrades?
Why does auth fail closed even when policies fail open?

question: Why is Redis used as the shared store for rate limiting here?
answer_hinglish:
Redis ek in-memory key-value store hai jo bahut fast hai (single digit millisecond ya usse kam typical latency), atomic operations deta hai, keys pe TTL laga sakta hai, aur server-side Lua scripts chala sakta hai. Rate limiting ke liye yeh chaaron cheezein exactly chahiye.

Problem yeh hai: app 3 replicas mein chal rahi hai (docker-compose mein api1, api2, api3 nginx ke peeche). Agar counter har server ki memory mein ho toh har server poori limit allow karega -- test `test_in_memory_limiter_overshoots_with_multiple_servers` exactly 3x overshoot prove karta hai. Isliye state ek central jagah chahiye jo saare instances dekh sakein.

Redis kyun, Postgres kyun nahi? Counter har request pe update hota hai; DB row lock aur disk write per request bahut mehenga hai. Rate limit state "soft state" hai -- kho jaye toh bas counters reset ho jaate hain, isliye durability ki zaroorat nahi. Aur TTL se purane counters apne aap delete ho jaate hain, koi cleanup job nahi.

Is project mein Redis mein chaar cheezein rehti hain: counters/buckets, policy overrides (`rl:config:policies`), hashed API keys (`rl:apikey:<sha256>`), aur Lua script cache.
why_needed: Multiple app servers ko ek hi global count dekhna hai, low latency ke saath, aur state automatically expire honi chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek shared whiteboard jo office ke har counter se dikhta hai -- har cashier wahin tally mark karta hai, apni personal diary mein nahi.
how_it_works: Har policy check ek EVALSHA call hai; Redis script ko single-threaded, bina interleaving ke chalata hai. Keys pe PEXPIRE lagta hai taaki idle identities khud saaf ho jayein.
in_this_project: `main.py` lifespan mein ek `Redis(connection_pool=BlockingConnectionPool...)` client banta hai aur `RedisRateLimiter`, `PolicyStore`, `ApiKeyStore` teeno usi ko share karte hain. Key layout `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` mein hai.
advantages: Saare instances ek truth dekhte hain
disadvantages: Single point of failure jab tak HA setup na ho
Har check pe network hop
common_mistakes: Rate limit counters ko durable DB mein rakhna
Redis ko shared maan ke non-atomic GET/SET karna
follow_up_questions: What happens if Redis goes down?
Why not Postgres with SELECT FOR UPDATE?
How would you shard Redis at 100x?

question: What is a Redis Lua script and why does it make the check atomic?
answer_hinglish:
Redis Lua script ek chhota program hai jo Redis server ke andar chalta hai. Jab Redis script execute karta hai, us dauraan koi doosri command (kisi bhi client ki) beech mein nahi chalti. Toh script ke andar "read state -> decide -> write state" ek single atomic step ban jata hai.

Rate limiting mein yahi chahiye. Agar hum client side pe pehle GET karein aur phir SET, toh do concurrent requests dono same purana count padh sakti hain aur dono allow ho jaati hain. Script mein yeh race possible hi nahi, kyunki Redis script ko poora chalata hai, phir agli command leta hai.

Is project mein har algorithm ki ek alag script hai: `fixed_window.lua`, `sliding_log.lua`, `sliding_counter.lua`, `token_bucket.lua`, `leaky_bucket.lua`. Sab ek hi contract follow karti hain: `KEYS[1]` base key, `ARGV` mein limit, window ya rate, `now_ms` (khaali ho toh Redis `TIME`), aur cost. Return hota hai `{allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reset_ms}`.

Ek bonus: ek hi network round-trip mein poora decision ho jata hai. WATCH/MULTI jaisa optimistic locking mein contention pe retries lagte hain, Lua mein nahi. Downside: script chalte waqt Redis block hota hai, isliye scripts O(1) ya O(log n) rakhni padti hain.
why_needed: Check-then-act ko atomic banana zaroori hai, warna concurrent requests limit cross kar deti hain.
real_world_analogy: ATM machine jo ek card ka transaction poora karke hi agla card leti hai -- beech mein koi aur balance nahi badal sakta.
how_it_works: Redis command execution single-threaded hai. EVAL/EVALSHA ek command hai; uske andar ke saare `redis.call` usi command ka hissa hain, isliye isolation milta hai.
in_this_project: `redis_limiter.py` mein `self._scripts = {alg: redis.register_script(_load(alg.value)) for alg in Algorithm}` -- har algorithm ka script ek baar load hota hai. `test_exact_under_concurrency_across_three_servers` 200 concurrent requests mein exactly 50 allowed prove karta hai.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: fixed_window.lua
local current = tonumber(redis.call('GET', key) or '0')
if current + cost > limit then
  return {0, math.max(limit - current, 0), reset_ms, reset_ms}
end
current = redis.call('INCRBY', key, cost)
advantages: Kisi bhi algorithm ke liye kaam karta hai
disadvantages: Script chalte waqt Redis blocked
Lua debug karna mushkil
Cluster mein saari keys ek slot mein honi chahiye
common_mistakes: Script mein lambi loops ya O(n) scans
Script ke bahar se time pass karna bina clock skew soche
follow_up_questions: What is EVALSHA and what happens on NOSCRIPT?
Why not WATCH/MULTI?
What limits does Redis Cluster put on scripts?

question: What do the RateLimit-*, X-RateLimit-* and Retry-After headers tell the client?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh headers client ko batate hain ki uska quota kitna hai, kitna bacha hai, aur kab reset hoga -- taaki achha client khud slow down kar sake bina 429 khaye.

Is project mein `rate_limit_headers` function yeh sab banata hai: `RateLimit-Limit` (binding policy ki limit), `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset` (seconds, ceil karke), aur `RateLimit-Policy` jaise `search_burst;alg=token_bucket`. Yeh IETF draft "RateLimit Fields for HTTP" ke style ke headers hain. Saath mein legacy `X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` bhi bhejte hain kyunki bahut saare clients wahi padhte hain. Agar Redis down tha aur policy fail-open hui toh `X-RateLimit-Status: degraded` add hota hai.

`Retry-After` sirf 429 ya 503 pe aata hai, whole seconds mein, aur minimum 1 -- `max((retry_after_ms + 999) // 1000, 1)`. 0 kabhi nahi bhejte kyunki "0 second baad retry" client ko tight loop mein daal deta hai.

Important subtlety: ek route pe multiple policies hain, toh headers kaunsi policy ke? `CombinedDecision.binding` decide karta hai -- deny hua toh sabse bada retry_after waali denial, warna sabse kam remaining waali policy. Test `test_headers_on_success` mein anonymous user ke liye limit 20 aata hai (user_plan), ip_global ka 300 nahi.
why_needed: Clients ko proactive backoff ke liye information chahiye; bina headers ke woh sirf 429 dekh ke guess karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Mobile data plan ka SMS: "aapka 1GB mein se 200MB bacha hai, reset kal raat 12 baje" -- aap khud usage adjust kar lete ho.
how_it_works: Lua script `{allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reset_ms}` return karta hai. Service `Decision` banata hai, binding choose karta hai, aur dependency `response.headers.update(headers)` karti hai; denial pe headers exception ke saath jaate hain.
in_this_project: `services/rate_limit_service.py::rate_limit_headers` aur `CombinedDecision.binding`; `deps.py` mein `response.headers.update(headers)`. Tests: `test_headers_on_success`, `test_429_with_retry_after_for_anonymous`.
advantages: Clients proactive backoff kar sakte hain
Debugging aasaan -- policy name header mein
disadvantages: Multiple policies ho toh sirf ek ki info dikhti hai
Headers thoda bandwidth lete hain
common_mistakes: Retry-After 0 bhejna
Reset ko absolute timestamp vs seconds mein confuse karna
Headers sirf 429 pe bhejna, 200 pe nahi
follow_up_questions: Why pick the policy with fewest remaining as binding?
Is RateLimit-Policy part of a standard?
What should a well-behaved client do with these headers?

question: What is the difference between per-IP, per-user and per-API-key scopes?
answer_hinglish:
Scope ka matlab hai counter kis identity pe key hoga. Is project mein `Scope` enum ke teen values hain: `ip`, `user`, `api_key`.

Per-IP: anonymous traffic aur abuse ke liye. `ip_global` aur `login_bruteforce` IP pe hain. Problem: ek office ke peeche 500 log ek hi NAT IP share karte hain, aur attacker IPs rotate kar sakta hai.

Per-user: subscription quota ke liye. Ek user ki chahe kitni bhi API keys hon, `user_plan` sab ka total ek counter mein count karta hai. Isse koi user naye keys bana ke quota bypass nahi kar sakta.

Per-API-key: har key ka apna bucket. `search_burst` per key hai -- matlab ek user ki do integrations (do keys) ek doosre ka burst nahi khaati.

Yeh fark test `test_user_quota_shared_across_keys_but_api_key_scope_is_per_key` prove karta hai: bob ki key 1 se 5 searches ke baad 429, lekin key 2 ka bucket fresh hai.

Ek edge case: anonymous caller user-scoped policy hit kare toh `user_id` None hai. `_identity_key` usse `anon-ip:<ip>` pe fall back karta hai, taaki "no key" ka matlab "no limit" na ho. Key format `ip:1.2.3.4`, `user:alice`, `api_key:3f9a...` hota hai.
why_needed: Alag threats aur business rules alag identity pe count hone chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Gym: building ka gate per person count karta hai (IP), membership plan per member (user), aur locker per locker-key (API key).
how_it_works: `Identity.key_for(scope)` dict lookup se ip/user_id/api_key_id return karta hai. Service usme scope prefix lagata hai aur Redis key `rl:<policy>:{<scope>:<id>}` banti hai.
in_this_project: `domain/models.py::Identity.key_for`, `services/rate_limit_service.py::_identity_key`. `policies.json` mein scopes: ip_global=ip, user_plan=user, search_burst=api_key, login_bruteforce=ip, reports_smooth=user.
advantages: Har threat ke liye sahi granularity
Key rotation se user quota bypass nahi hota
disadvantages: IP scope NAT ke peeche users ko unfair hit karta hai
Per-IP limit IP rotation se bypass hota hai
common_mistakes: Anonymous caller ko user policy se chhoot dena
Scope prefix ke bina key banana (ip aur user ids collide ho sakte hain)
follow_up_questions: How do you stop an attacker rotating IPs?
Why is search_burst per key and not per user?
What about IPv6?

question: Explain the fixed window algorithm and its boundary burst weakness.
answer_hinglish:
Fixed window mein time ko fixed slots mein baant dete hain, jaise har minute 00 se 59 second tak. Har slot ka ek counter hai; counter limit tak pahuncha toh baaki requests us slot ke end tak reject.

`fixed_window.lua` mein `window_start = now - (now % window)` slot nikalta hai aur key `KEYS[1]:window_start` banti hai. Pehle GET karke check karte hain `current + cost > limit`; agar haan toh reject (aur rejected request count nahi hoti), warna INCRBY, aur pehli increment pe PEXPIRE window.

Weakness: boundary burst. Limit 3/second hai. Client 999ms pe 3 requests bhejta hai (window 1 khatam hone wali hai) aur 1000ms pe 3 aur (naya window). Dono windows apni jagah sahi hain, lekin 2 milliseconds mein 6 requests pass -- limit ka 2x. Test `test_boundary_burst_weakness` exactly yahi prove karta hai.

Phir bhi use kyun? Yeh sabse simple aur sasta hai -- O(1) memory, ek key per identity per window. Subscription quota jaise "60 per minute" ke liye users ko yeh samajh bhi aata hai. Isliye `user_plan` fixed window use karta hai. Jahan exactness chahiye (login) wahan sliding log hai.
why_needed: Simple, cheap quota enforcement ke liye; boundary weakness samajhna zaroori hai taaki galat jagah use na ho.
real_world_analogy: Daily ATM limit jo raat 12 baje reset hoti hai: 11:59 pe poora nikalo, 12:01 pe phir poora -- 2 minute mein double.
how_it_works: Window id = floor(now/window)*window. Counter key mein window id hai, isliye naya window = naya key = count 0. Purani key PEXPIRE se expire.
in_this_project: `lua/fixed_window.lua`; policy `user_plan` (anonymous 20/min, free 60, pro 600, enterprise 6000). Tests: `TestFixedWindow` -- retry_after 900ms check, denied requests count nahi hote, boundary burst.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_algorithms.py
async def test_boundary_burst_weakness(self, redis):
    lim, p = RedisRateLimiter(redis), make_policy(Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW, 3, window=1)
    late = [await run(lim, p, T0 + 999) for _ in range(3)]
    early = [await run(lim, p, T0 + 1000) for _ in range(3)]
    assert all(r.allowed for r in late + early)
advantages: Samajhne aur explain karne mein aasaan
disadvantages: Boundary pe 2x burst
Window start pe thundering herd (sab clients ek saath reset dekhte hain)
common_mistakes: Window ko request ke first time se start karna aur phir bhi fixed window bolna
TTL na lagana -- keys hamesha rehti hain
follow_up_questions: How does sliding log fix the boundary burst?
Why did you not count rejected requests?
Where is the 2x burst acceptable?

question: How does the sliding window log work and why is it used for login?
answer_hinglish:
Sliding log har accepted request ka timestamp ek Redis sorted set (ZSET) mein store karta hai, score = timestamp ms. Har check pe pehle window se purane entries hata do (`ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf now-window`), phir `ZCARD` se count lo. `count + cost > limit` toh reject, warna ZADD karo.

Yeh exact hai: kisi bhi window-length ke period mein kabhi limit se zyada requests nahi jaati. Boundary burst nahi hota -- `test_no_boundary_burst` mein 999ms pe 3 allowed, 1000ms pe teeno denied, kyunki pichhle 3 abhi bhi last 1 second mein hain.

Retry-after bhi exact hai: sabse purani entry (`ZRANGE key 0 0 WITHSCORES`) jab window se bahar jayegi tab slot khulega. Test mein 0,100,200 pe requests ke baad 300 pe deny aur retry_after 700ms.

Cost: memory O(limit) per identity, kyunki har request ek member hai. Isliye `login_bruteforce` ke liye perfect -- limit sirf 5/min hai, toh max 5 members, aur login pe exactness matter karta hai (2x burst matlab double password guesses). Per-IP global limit 300/min pe lakhon IPs ke liye yeh mehenga hota, wahan sliding counter use kiya.

Ek detail: member unique hona chahiye, warna same millisecond ki do requests ek hi member overwrite karti. Isliye Python har call pe `uuid.uuid4().hex` ARGV[5] mein bhejta hai.
why_needed: Jahan limit chhoti ho aur exactness security ke liye zaroori ho (brute force), wahan approximation acceptable nahi.
real_world_analogy: Club ka bouncer jo har aane wale ka entry time register mein likhta hai aur check karta hai "pichhle 60 minute mein 5 se zyada toh nahi aaye?" -- har baar purane naam kaat deta hai.
how_it_works: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE O(log N + M), ZCARD O(1), ZADD O(log N). Members score se sorted hain isliye oldest nikalna O(log N).
in_this_project: `lua/sliding_log.lua`; `redis_limiter.py::_args` mein `args.append(uuid.uuid4().hex)`. Policy `login_bruteforce`: 5 per 60s per IP, `fail_mode: closed`. Tests: `TestSlidingLog`.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: sliding_log.lua
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', now - window)
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count + cost > limit then
  local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGE', KEYS[1], 0, 0, 'WITHSCORES')
  ...
end
for i = 1, cost do
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], now, ARGV[5] .. ':' .. i)
end
disadvantages: O(limit) memory per identity
Badi limits pe script heavy ho jati hai
common_mistakes: Timestamp ko hi member bana dena (same ms collisions)
Badi limit (jaise 10000/min) pe sliding log lagana
follow_up_questions: Why not use sliding log for ip_global?
What is the time complexity of the script?
How is retry-after computed when cost > 1?

question: How does the sliding window counter approximate a sliding window?
answer_hinglish:
Sliding counter do fixed windows ke counters rakhta hai -- current aur previous -- aur ek weighted estimate banata hai: `estimated = cur + prev * (window - elapsed) / window`. Assumption yeh hai ki previous window ka traffic evenly spread tha, toh jitna hissa previous window ka abhi bhi "sliding" window ke andar hai, utna share count karo.

Example test `test_weights_previous_window` se: limit 10/second. T0+500 pe 10 requests allowed (previous window full). Ab T0+1250 pe hum naye window mein 25% andar hain, toh weight 0.75, estimate = 0 + 10*0.75 = 7.5. Pehli request: 7.5+1 = 8.5 <= 10 allowed. Doosri: 1+7.5+1 = 9.5 allowed. Teesri: 2+7.5+1 = 10.5 denied. Result `[True, True, False]`.

Fayda: O(1) memory -- sirf do integers per identity, sliding log ki tarah har request ka timestamp nahi. Fixed window ka 2x boundary burst bhi mostly smooth ho jata hai. Yeh approach Cloudflare ne publicly describe ki thi.

Nuksaan: approximate hai. Agar previous window ka saara traffic uske end mein aaya tha toh estimate kam aayega aur thoda overshoot ho sakta hai. Isliye `ip_global` (huge key space, approx chalega) pe use kiya, login pe nahi. Load test mein minute boundary cross karne waale run mein 315 allowed aaye -- yeh bug nahi, naye window ka legitimate share tha.
why_needed: Lakhon IPs ke liye exact log mehenga hai; O(1) memory ke saath fixed window se behtar accuracy chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Highway toll ka estimate: "pichhle ghante 100 gaadiyan aayi, is ghante ke 15 minute mein 20 -- toh last 60 minute mein roughly 20 + 100*0.75 = 95".
how_it_works: Do keys `KEYS[1]:cur_start` aur `KEYS[1]:prev_start`. Allowed hone pe sirf current INCRBY, aur PEXPIRE 2*window taaki agle window mein yeh previous ki tarah padhi ja sake.
in_this_project: `lua/sliding_counter.lua`; policy `ip_global` (300/60s per IP). Tests: `test_weights_previous_window`, `test_previous_window_fully_expires`. TESTING.md ka 315-allowed observation.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: sliding_counter.lua
local elapsed = now - cur_start
local weight = (window - elapsed) / window
local estimated = cur + prev * weight
if estimated + cost > limit then ... end
cur = redis.call('INCRBY', cur_key, cost)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', cur_key, window * 2)
disadvantages: Approximate; uneven traffic pe slight overshoot/undershoot
Retry-after bhi estimate hai
common_mistakes: Previous key ko sirf 1 window ka TTL dena -- agle window mein woh gayab ho jayegi
Approximation ko exact claim karna
follow_up_questions: When can the estimate be wrong and by how much?
Why does the script touch two keys and what does that mean for Redis Cluster?
How is retry-after computed here?

question: Explain the token bucket algorithm and lazy refill.
answer_hinglish:
Token bucket mein har identity ka ek bucket hai jisme max `capacity` tokens aa sakte hain, aur bucket `rate` tokens per second se refill hota hai. Har request `cost` tokens leti hai. Tokens hain toh allow, warna reject. Naya identity full bucket se start karta hai, isliye shuru mein capacity tak ka burst allowed hai, phir steady rate.

"Lazy refill" ka matlab: koi background timer nahi chalta jo har second tokens daale. Jab request aati hai tab hum calculate karte hain ki last update (`ts`) se ab tak kitne tokens "bhar gaye honge": `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * rate / 1000)`. Lakhon buckets ke liye timers impossible hain; lazy calculation O(1) hai.

`token_bucket.lua` state ek hash mein rakhta hai `{tokens, ts}`. Tokens fractional ho sakte hain aur `tostring` se full precision store hote hain -- test `test_fractional_refill_is_preserved` mein 500ms pe 0.5 token (deny) aur 1000ms pe 0.5+0.5 = 1 (allow); rounding se token khota nahi.

Retry-after: `ceil((cost - tokens) * 1000 / rate)`. Test `test_cost_greater_than_one`: capacity 10, rate 1, pehli cost-7 request ke baad 3 bache, doosri cost-7 ko 4 aur chahiye toh retry 4000ms.

Is project mein `search_burst` token bucket hai: free plan capacity 5, refill 0.5/s -- search mehenga hai, thoda burst chalega lekin sustained flood nahi.
why_needed: Real clients bursty hote hain (page load pe 5 calls ek saath); token bucket burst allow karta hai aur long-term rate cap karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Metro card jisme har ghante kuch balance automatically add hota hai, max limit tak. Ek din zyada travel kar sakte ho jab tak balance hai, phir refill ki speed se hi.
how_it_works: Hash fields `tokens` aur `ts`; har call pe refill compute, decide, HSET, aur PEXPIRE `ceil(capacity*1000/rate)+1000` -- itne time mein bucket waise bhi full ho jata, toh state delete karna safe hai.
in_this_project: `lua/token_bucket.lua`; policy `search_burst` scope api_key; plans free 5@0.5/s, pro 30@5/s, enterprise 100@20/s. Tests: `TestTokenBucket`, `test_keys_expire`.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: token_bucket.lua
local elapsed = math.max(now - ts, 0)
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * rate / 1000)
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retry = math.ceil((cost - tokens) * 1000 / rate)
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', tostring(now))
disadvantages: Do parameters (capacity, rate) tune karne padte hain
Burst downstream pe spike la sakta hai
common_mistakes: Tokens ko integer mein round karna -- fractional refill kho jata hai
Background job se refill karna
`elapsed` negative hone dena (clock jump)

What is GCRA?
Why is the TTL capacity/rate + 1s?

question: What is the difference between token bucket and leaky bucket in this project?
answer_hinglish:
Dono O(1) aur rate-based hain, lekin semantics ulte hain. Token bucket mein bucket tokens se bhara hota hai aur request tokens nikalti hai; idle time mein tokens jama hote hain, toh burst allowed hai. Leaky bucket ("meter" variant) mein request bucket mein paani daalti hai aur paani constant `leak_per_sec` se nikalta hai; overflow hua toh reject.

Maths mein dono kaafi similar dikhte hain -- dono ka capacity burst tolerance deta hai. Practical fark yeh hai ki leaky bucket ko hum "downstream ko smooth rate do" ke mindset se use karte hain: `reports_smooth` policy free/default ke liye capacity 3 aur leak 0.2/s hai, matlab report service ko sustained 1 report per 5 second se zyada nahi milega. Token bucket (`search_burst`) ka focus "burst chalega, average cap karo" hai.

Ek important honest point: is project ka leaky bucket "meter" variant hai -- overflow pe reject karta hai. Classic "leaky bucket as a queue" variant request ko queue mein rakh ke constant rate pe process karta (delay karta, reject nahi). Woh is project mein implement nahi hai; README ke known limitations mein likha hai.

Test `test_smooth_rate`: capacity 3, rate 1 -- 3 allowed, chautha deny with retry 1000ms, 1 second baad ek unit leak hua toh ek aur allowed, phir deny.
why_needed: Interviewers aksar dono ko confuse karte hain; sahi distinction aur "meter vs queue" batana maturity dikhata hai.
real_world_analogy: Token bucket: piggy bank jisme roz paise aate hain, ek din saare kharch kar sakte ho. Leaky bucket: neeche chhed wali balti -- kitna bhi daalo, neeche se ek hi speed se nikalta hai; zyada daala toh upar se gir jata hai.
how_it_works: Leaky: `level = max(0, level - elapsed*rate/1000)`; `level + cost <= capacity` toh allow aur level badhao; retry `ceil((level+cost-capacity)*1000/rate)`. Token: `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed*rate/1000)`.
in_this_project: `lua/leaky_bucket.lua` (hash `{level, ts}`), `lua/token_bucket.lua` (hash `{tokens, ts}`). Policies: `reports_smooth` (leaky, scope user) aur `search_burst` (token, scope api_key).
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: leaky_bucket.lua
level = math.max(0, level - elapsed * rate / 1000)
if level + cost <= capacity then
  level = level + cost
  allowed = 1
else
  retry = math.ceil((level + cost - capacity) * 1000 / rate)
end
disadvantages: Meter variant request delay nahi karta, reject karta hai
Queue variant ke liye extra infra (queue/worker) chahiye
common_mistakes: Kehna ki leaky bucket burst bilkul allow nahi karta -- meter variant capacity tak karta hai
Queue aur meter variant ko mix karna
follow_up_questions: How would you implement the queue variant?
Are token bucket and leaky bucket (meter) mathematically equivalent?
Which one protects a slow downstream better?

question: How did you choose which algorithm to use for each policy?
answer_hinglish:
Maine har policy ke liye teen sawaal pooche: kitni identities hongi (memory), exactness kitni zaroori hai, aur burst chahiye ya smoothness.

`ip_global` -- har IP pe 300/min, key space huge (lakhon IPs). Exactness critical nahi, memory critical hai. Isliye sliding counter: O(1), boundary burst smooth.

`user_plan` -- subscription quota "60 per minute". Users ko simple mental model chahiye aur boundary ka 2x burst business ke liye acceptable hai. Isliye fixed window: sabse sasta.

`login_bruteforce` -- 5 attempts/min per IP. Limit chhoti hai toh sliding log ki O(limit) memory sirf 5 entries hai, aur exactness security ke liye zaroori hai. Plus fail-closed.

`search_burst` -- search mehenga hai lekin clients bursty hain. Token bucket: capacity tak burst, phir refill rate.

`reports_smooth` -- report generation ek slow downstream ko hit karta hai jise smooth rate chahiye. Leaky bucket (meter).

Yeh table `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ke "Algorithm choice guide" mein hai. Interview mein main yeh bolta hoon: "Koi ek best algorithm nahi hai; maine use case ke hisaab se trade-off choose kiya, aur saare 5 ek hi contract follow karte hain toh policy change karna sirf JSON edit hai."
why_needed: Galat algorithm ya toh memory waste karta hai ya security gap chhodta hai.
real_world_analogy: Alag darwazon ke liye alag taale: main gate pe simple counter, locker pe exact register, canteen pe token system.
how_it_works: Policy JSON mein `algorithm` field enum hai; `RedisRateLimiter` us enum se script choose karta hai, aur `_args` window ya rate pass karta hai.
in_this_project: `policies.json` ke 5 policies aur `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka algorithm table. `Policy._check_params` ensure karta hai ki windowed algorithms ko `window_seconds` aur buckets ko `rate_per_second` mile.
advantages: Har use case ka optimal trade-off
Runtime pe algorithm switch possible (admin PUT)
disadvantages: 5 algorithms maintain aur test karne padte hain
Ops team ko har ek ka semantics samajhna padta hai
common_mistakes: Har jagah ek hi algorithm lagana
Badi limit pe sliding log lagana
follow_up_questions: Can you change a policy's algorithm at runtime?
What happens to existing state when the algorithm changes?
Which would you pick for a webhook sender?

question: Why does an in-memory rate limiter fail when you run multiple servers?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki har server ki apni memory hai aur load balancer requests ko servers mein baant deta hai. Server 1 ko user ki ek-tihaai requests dikhti hain, Server 2 ko alag ek-tihaai. Har server sochta hai "abhi limit nahi aayi", aur total allowed = N servers x limit.

Maine yeh test se prove kiya. `test_in_memory_limiter_overshoots_with_multiple_servers` mein 3 `InMemoryRateLimiter` instances hain (3 servers), limit 50, aur 200 requests round-robin (`servers[i % 3]`). Assertion hai `sum(allowed) == LIMIT * 3` -- exactly 150. Matlab user ko 3x quota mil gaya.

`memory_limiter.py` code galat nahi hai -- ek process ke liye bilkul sahi hai, `asyncio.Lock` se event loop ke andar interleaving bhi protected hai. Problem architecture ki hai: state local hai. Isliye maine yeh file "teaching contrast" ke roop mein rakhi hai, production mein use nahi hoti.

Fix: state ko shared store (Redis) mein le jao. Lekin sirf shared karna kaafi nahi -- naive GET/SET bhi race karta hai. Isliye atomic Lua script. Interview line: "Maine test likh ke prove kiya ki local counters 3 servers pe exactly 3x overshoot karte hain, aur Lua limiter usi setup mein exactly 50 allow karta hai."
why_needed: Horizontal scaling ke saath local state galat ho jati hai; yeh distributed limiter ka basic motivation hai.
real_world_analogy: Teen alag gate pe teen guard, har ek ke paas apna register: "har aadmi 5 baar andar aa sakta hai". Ek aadmi teeno gates se 5-5 baar aa gaya -- 15.
how_it_works: Counter key `policy:key:window_start` ek Python dict mein hai; dict process-local hai, servers ke beech share nahi hota.
in_this_project: `limiter/memory_limiter.py::InMemoryRateLimiter` (sirf fixed_window aur token_bucket support), `tests/test_distributed_correctness.py`.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_distributed_correctness.py
servers = [InMemoryRateLimiter() for _ in range(3)]  # each server has its own memory
results = await asyncio.gather(*[servers[i % 3].check("u", policy, policy.default, now_ms=T0)
                                 for i in range(REQUESTS)])
assert sum(r.allowed for r in results) == LIMIT * 3
disadvantages: Fleet mein N x overshoot
Restart pe state lost
Autoscaling se limit badalti rehti hai
common_mistakes: Sticky sessions se fix karne ki koshish -- user multiple IPs/devices se aa sakta hai
Limit ko N se divide karna jab N dynamic hai
follow_up_questions: Could you divide the limit by the number of servers?
Is the in-memory limiter useful anywhere?
Why does shared Redis alone not fix it?

question: What is a check-then-act race condition and how does the naive Redis limiter show it?
answer_hinglish:
Check-then-act race tab hoti hai jab hum pehle state padhte hain (check), uske basis pe decide karte hain, aur phir alag step mein likhte hain (act). Dono steps ke beech koi aur actor state badal sakta hai, toh decision purane data pe hota hai.

`naive_redis_limiter.py` exactly yeh karta hai: `current = GET key`, `if current + cost > limit: deny`, warna `SET key current+cost`. Do requests ek saath aati hain, dono `4` padhti hain (limit 5), dono sochti hain jagah hai, dono `5` likhti hain. Dono allowed, aur counter 6 hona chahiye tha par 5 hai -- ek increment "lost update" ho gaya.

Interesting baat: Redis shared hai aur Redis ki har command atomic hai. Phir bhi galat, kyunki atomicity ek command ki hai, do commands ke sequence ki nahi. Do `await` ke beech event loop doosre coroutines chala deta hai.

Test `test_naive_get_then_set_on_shared_redis_overshoots` 200 concurrent requests (limit 50) bhejta hai aur assert karta hai `allowed > LIMIT`. Exact number har run mein alag hota hai -- isliye test exact number nahi, sirf overshoot assert karta hai.

Fix options: INCR-first (pehle increment, phir compare -- atomic lekin rejected bhi count hote hain), WATCH/MULTI (retries), ya Lua script (read+decide+write ek step). Maine Lua choose kiya.
why_needed: Yeh samjhe bina log "Redis use kar raha hoon, toh distributed safe hai" maan lete hain.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek hi bank account se ek saath ATM pe 500 nikalte hain; dono machines ne balance 600 dekha, dono ne 500 diya. Balance check aur debit ek atomic step hona chahiye tha.
how_it_works: Interleaving: A.GET(4) -> B.GET(4) -> A.SET(5) -> B.SET(5). Dono `await` points pe event loop switch kar sakta hai, aur alag connections pe Redis bhi commands interleave karta hai.
in_this_project: `limiter/naive_redis_limiter.py::NaiveRedisFixedWindow` -- comment mein race window marked hai: "race window between these two awaits". Test client ko `max_connections=REQUESTS` diya taaki saari requests parallel jaayein.
disadvantages: Concurrency mein overshoot
Lost updates -- counter actual se kam
common_mistakes: Sochna ki single-threaded Redis automatically compound logic ko safe bana deta hai
Pipeline (non-transactional) ko atomic samajhna
follow_up_questions: How does INCR-first fix it and what is its drawback?
Would MULTI/EXEC alone fix it?
Why does the test assert > LIMIT instead of an exact number?

question: Why do the Lua scripts use Redis TIME instead of the application server's clock?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki multiple app servers ki ghadiyan kabhi perfectly sync nahi hoti. NTP ke saath bhi tens of milliseconds ka skew normal hai, aur VM pause ya galat NTP config pe seconds tak. Agar Server A ki ghadi 2 second aage hai, toh woh naya window pehle shuru maan lega, aur token bucket mein `elapsed` zyada calculate karke extra tokens de dega. Same identity ke liye do servers alag "now" bhejenge toh state (`ts`) aage-peeche hoti rahegi.

Solution: saari scripts mein `if ARGV[3] == '' then local t = redis.call('TIME') ...`. Redis ki ek hi ghadi sab instances ke liye single source of truth hai, toh skew ka sawaal hi khatam. FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md ke scenario 9 mein yahi likha hai: "Clock skew between app servers -- irrelevant".

Tests mein `now_ms` explicitly pass karte hain (`T0 = 1_700_000_000_000`) taaki results deterministic hon, aur ek test `test_uses_redis_server_time_when_now_not_given` server-time path bhi verify karta hai.

Trade-off: `TIME` call script ko non-deterministic banata hai. Purane Redis (< 5) mein script replication verbatim hota tha, toh replica pe alag time aata; `redis.replicate_commands()` chahiye tha. Redis 7 effects replication use karta hai (script ke writes replicate hote hain), toh problem nahi. Bhi dhyan rahe: Redis ka clock bhi jump kar sakta hai, isliye scripts mein `math.max(now - ts, 0)` hai taaki negative elapsed se tokens kam na hon.
why_needed: Distributed system mein time ek shared resource hai; window boundaries aur refill sab time pe depend karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Teen alag dukaanon ki ghadiyan alag time dikhati hain, toh "dukaan 9 baje band" ka matlab har jagah alag. Ek central clock tower sab ke liye ek time.
how_it_works: `TIME` seconds aur microseconds return karta hai; script `t[1]*1000 + floor(t[2]/1000)` se ms banati hai. Python `now_ms=None` pe ARGV[3] khaali string bhejta hai.
in_this_project: Har `.lua` file ki top lines; `redis_limiter.py::_args` mein `now = "" if now_ms is None else str(now_ms)`. TRADEOFFS.md #3.
code_example:
-- real: every script
local now
if ARGV[3] == '' then
  local t = redis.call('TIME')
  now = tonumber(t[1]) * 1000 + math.floor(tonumber(t[2]) / 1000)
else
  now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
end
disadvantages: Script non-deterministic (purane Redis mein replication issue)
Redis Cluster mein alag shards ki alag ghadiyan
common_mistakes: App server ka time.time() script mein pass karna production mein
Negative elapsed handle na karna
follow_up_questions: What happens in Redis Cluster where each shard has its own clock?
What did Redis < 5 need for scripts that call TIME?
What if Redis' own clock jumps backwards?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Central clock (Redis) vs app clock: Redis TIME skew khatam karta hai lekin ek aur Redis call script ke andar. App clock pass karna deterministic hai lekin skew ka risk. Project ne default Redis TIME aur tests ke liye injection choose kiya -- dono ka fayda.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Failover pe naye primary ki ghadi thodi alag ho sakti hai; agar woh peeche hai toh `elapsed` negative aata, jise `math.max(now - ts, 0)` 0 kar deta hai, matlab thodi der refill ruk jata hai -- safe side. Aage hai toh thode extra tokens.
advanced.alternatives: Hybrid logical clocks, ya app servers pe chrony/PTP se tight sync aur app time pass karna. GCRA mein bhi time hi state hai, wahi skew issue.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Cluster mode mein har key ek shard pe hai aur us shard ka TIME use hota hai; ek identity ka state ek shard pe rehta hai, toh consistency per-identity bani rehti hai. 100x pe bhi yeh design theek hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Redis hosts pe NTP monitoring, clock jump ka alert, aur failover ke baad skew check. Version pin karo (Redis 7) taaki effects replication guaranteed ho.

question: Walk through fixed_window.lua line by line.
answer_hinglish:
Script ka contract: `KEYS[1]` base key (jaise `rl:user_plan:{ip:1.2.3.4}`), `ARGV[1]` limit, `ARGV[2]` window ms, `ARGV[3]` now (khaali = Redis TIME), `ARGV[4]` cost. Return `{allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reset_ms}`.

Step 1: `now` nikalo -- injected ya `TIME` se.

Step 2: `window_start = now - (now % window)`. Yeh epoch-aligned window hai, toh saare servers aur saari identities ke windows same boundaries pe hain. Actual key = `KEYS[1] .. ':' .. window_start`, toh har window ki alag key.

Step 3: `reset_ms = window_start + window - now` -- window khatam hone mein kitna time.

Step 4: `GET` current count. Agar `current + cost > limit` toh `{0, max(limit - current, 0), reset_ms, reset_ms}` return. Note: rejected request count NAHI hoti. Test `test_denied_requests_are_not_counted` 5 rejected requests ke baad bhi key value 1 assert karta hai.

Step 5: warna `INCRBY key cost`. Agar result `== cost` hai matlab yeh key abhi bani hai, toh `PEXPIRE key window`. TTL sirf pehli baar lagta hai -- har request pe TTL reset karne se window "slide" karne lagti.

Step 6: `{1, limit - current, 0, reset_ms}`.

Kyun GET phir INCRBY, sirf INCR-first kyun nahi? Kyunki INCR-first rejected requests bhi count kar deta aur decrement karna padta. Script ke andar GET+INCRBY atomic hai, toh koi race nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer aksar ek script pe deep dive maangta hai; sabse simple script se line-level understanding dikhana easy hai.
real_world_analogy: Har ghante ki ek nayi register sheet: sheet pe ghante ka naam likha hai, ghanta khatam to sheet phenk do.
how_it_works: Epoch-aligned windows + per-window keys + first-write TTL. Atomicity Lua se, isliye GET aur INCRBY ke beech koi aur client nahi aata.
in_this_project: `limiter/lua/fixed_window.lua`; test `test_allows_limit_then_denies_until_window_end` mein limit 3, window 1s, T0+100 pe 4 requests: remaining [2,1,0], chauthi deny with retry 900ms.
code_example:
-- real: fixed_window.lua (core)
local window_start = now - (now % window)
local key = KEYS[1] .. ':' .. window_start
local reset_ms = window_start + window - now
local current = tonumber(redis.call('GET', key) or '0')
if current + cost > limit then
  return {0, math.max(limit - current, 0), reset_ms, reset_ms}
end
current = redis.call('INCRBY', key, cost)
if current == cost then
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
end
return {1, limit - current, 0, reset_ms}
disadvantages: Key name script ke andar banta hai (KEYS[1] + suffix) -- strictly Redis docs kehte hain saari keys KEYS mein pass karo
common_mistakes: Har INCR pe PEXPIRE lagana (window slide ho jata hai)
TTL bhool jana
follow_up_questions: Accessing a key not passed in KEYS -- is that a problem in Redis Cluster?
How would you count rejected requests?
Why is the window epoch-aligned?

question: How does sliding_counter.lua compute retry-after when a request is denied?
answer_hinglish:
Deny hone pe sawaal yeh hai: kab tak wait karein ki estimate itna gir jaye ki yeh request fit ho jaye? Sliding counter mein estimate `cur + prev * weight` hai, aur jaise time aage badhta hai `weight` linearly 1 se 0 tak girta hai. Matlab previous window ka contribution har millisecond `prev / window` kam hota hai.

Script yeh karti hai: default `retry = window - elapsed` (current window ke end tak, jab previous poora bahar ho jayega). Agar `prev > 0` hai toh `needed = estimated + cost - limit` -- kitna weighted count gayab hona chahiye. Us ke liye `ms = ceil(needed / prev * window)`. Agar yeh chhota hai toh woh use karo. Final `max(retry, 1)` taaki 0 kabhi return na ho.

Example: limit 10, window 1000ms, prev = 10, cur = 2, elapsed 250 -> estimate 9.5. Ek request (cost 1): needed = 0.5, ms = ceil(0.5/10*1000) = 50ms. 50ms baad weight 0.70, estimate 9.0, aur 9.0+1 = 10 fit.

Honest caveat: yeh estimate assume karta hai ki current window mein beech mein koi naya traffic nahi aayega. Agar aaya toh client ko phir 429 milega -- isliye Retry-After ek hint hai, guarantee nahi. Aur current-window ka hissa kabhi decay nahi hota, toh agar `cur + cost > limit` hai toh sirf next window hi help karega -- default retry yahi cover karta hai.
why_needed: Accurate Retry-After clients ko unnecessary retries aur unnecessary wait dono se bachata hai.
real_world_analogy: Paani ki tanki jo dheere-dheere khali ho rahi hai: kitni der baad itni jagah banegi ki ek balti aur aa jaye -- drain rate se calculate karo.
how_it_works: Linear decay of prev contribution: d(estimate)/dt = -prev/window. Required drop / rate = time. Ceil + min with end-of-window bound.
in_this_project: `lua/sliding_counter.lua` lines with `needed` aur `ms`; return `{0, remaining, max(retry,1), window - elapsed}`. Retry ms service mein seconds mein ceil hota hai (`raise_if_denied`).
code_example:
-- real: sliding_counter.lua
if estimated + cost > limit then
  local retry = window - elapsed
  if prev > 0 then
    local needed = estimated + cost - limit
    local ms = math.ceil(needed / prev * window)
    if ms < retry then retry = ms end
  end
  return {0, math.max(math.floor(limit - estimated), 0), math.max(retry, 1), window - elapsed}
end
advantages: Tight retry estimate, unnecessarily lamba wait nahi
disadvantages: Assumption: beech mein naya traffic nahi
HTTP Retry-After seconds mein hai, toh ms precision kho jati hai
common_mistakes: Retry = window - elapsed hamesha dena (bahut pessimistic)
Division by zero jab prev = 0 -- script isse guard karti hai
follow_up_questions: Is Retry-After a promise?
How do clients add jitter?
What happens if cur alone already exceeds the limit?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Exact retry (sliding log) memory maangta hai; approximate (sliding counter) O(1) hai lekin hint hi hai. Project ne ip_global ke liye approximate accept kiya.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Bahut saare clients same retry_after pe wapas aayen toh synchronized retry storm; server side mein jitter nahi hai, client ko add karna chahiye.
advanced.alternatives: Retry ko simply window end tak set karna (simple, pessimistic), ya token bucket jaisa exact model use karna.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x pe retry storms real problem hain -- Retry-After ke saath jitter recommend karo, ya server randomised retry de.
advanced.production_improvements: Retry-After ke saath `RateLimit-Reset` bhi diya hai; production mein client SDK mein exponential backoff + jitter documented karo.

question: Walk through sliding_log.lua and explain why each request needs a unique member.
answer_hinglish:
Script ka flow: (1) `now` nikalo. (2) `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf now-window` -- jo entries window se bahar slide ho gayi unko hata do. (3) `ZCARD` se current count. (4) Agar `count + cost > limit` toh deny: oldest entry `ZRANGE key 0 0 WITHSCORES` nikalo, retry = `oldest + window - now` (minimum 1). (5) Warna `for i = 1, cost` ZADD karo score `now` aur member `ARGV[5] .. ':' .. i`. (6) `PEXPIRE key window`. (7) `{1, limit - count - cost, 0, window}` return.

Unique member kyun? ZSET mein member unique hota hai; same member dobara ZADD karo toh sirf score update hota hai, count nahi badhta. Agar hum member = timestamp rakhte, toh same millisecond mein aayi do requests (concurrency mein bahut common) ek hi entry ban jaati -- limiter ek request "bhool" jata aur overshoot karta. Isliye `redis_limiter.py::_args` har call pe `uuid.uuid4().hex` ARGV[5] mein bhejta hai, aur cost > 1 pe `:1`, `:2` suffix lagta hai.

Distributed correctness test mein 200 requests same `now_ms=T0 + 5` ke saath jaati hain -- sab same score. Unique members ki wajah se hi exactly 50 allowed aata hai.

PEXPIRE window kyun? Agar identity window bhar idle rahe toh saari entries waise bhi expire ho chuki hoti, toh poora key drop karna safe hai.
why_needed: ZSET semantics ka subtle bug (duplicate members) concurrency mein silently limit tod deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Register mein sirf time likhoge toh ek hi minute mein aaye do log ek line ban jayenge. Har visitor ka token number bhi likho.
how_it_works: ZSET = skiplist + hash; score se range ops O(log N + M). Member uniqueness hash se.
in_this_project: `lua/sliding_log.lua`, `redis_limiter.py` mein `args.append(uuid.uuid4().hex)  # unique ZSET member per request`. Login policy limit 5 -- max 5 members.
advantages: Exact counting even with identical timestamps
disadvantages: uuid generation + bada member size (memory)
cost > 1 pe cost ZADD calls
common_mistakes: Timestamp ko member banana
Cleanup (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE) bhool jana -- set badhta rahega
follow_up_questions: Could you generate the unique id inside Lua?
What does the script return as reset_ms on allow?
What is the worst-case script cost?

question: How does token_bucket.lua handle fractional tokens, TTL and retry-after for cost > 1?
answer_hinglish:
Teen subtle details hain jo is script ko correct banati hain.

Fractional tokens: refill `elapsed * rate / 1000` fractional hota hai (rate 0.5/s pe 100ms mein 0.05 token). Agar hum tokens ko integer mein store karte toh har baar fraction kho jata aur slow-rate plans pe bucket kabhi refill hi nahi hota. Script `HSET ... 'tokens', tostring(tokens)` se full precision store karti hai. Test `test_fractional_refill_is_preserved`: capacity 1, rate 1 -- T0 allow, T0+500 deny (0.5 token), T0+1000 allow (0.5+0.5). Client ko `remaining` mein `math.floor(tokens)` dikhta hai, internally fraction rehta hai.

TTL: `PEXPIRE key ceil(capacity * 1000 / rate) + 1000`. Logic: itne time mein bucket khali se poora bhar jata, toh agar identity itni der idle rahe toh state ka koi matlab nahi -- missing key = full bucket (`tokens == nil` pe `tokens = capacity`). Result same, memory free. +1000ms safety margin. `test_keys_expire` capacity 2 rate 1 pe `0 < pttl <= 3000` check karta hai.

Retry-after with cost: `ceil((cost - tokens) * 1000 / rate)`. Test `test_cost_greater_than_one`: capacity 10, rate 1; cost 7 allow (3 bache); doosri cost 7 deny with remaining 3 aur retry 4000ms. Note: deny pe bhi state likhi jati hai (refilled tokens + ts=now) -- yeh correct hai kyunki refill already calculate ho chuka.

Edge: agar cost > capacity ho toh request kabhi allow nahi hogi, retry misleading hoga -- is project mein cost route-level constant hai, toh woh case nahi aata.
why_needed: Precision aur TTL bugs production mein subtle "limit kabhi refill nahi hoti" ya memory leak ban jate hain.
real_world_analogy: Rupees aur paise: agar har baar paise round off karo toh mahine ke end tak bahut paisa gayab.
how_it_works: Lua numbers doubles hain; `tostring` precision theek-thaak rakhta hai. Missing state = full bucket ka invariant TTL ko safe banata hai.
in_this_project: `lua/token_bucket.lua` ke comments: "Store state with full precision" aur "After capacity/rate seconds the bucket is full again, so state can be dropped".
code_example:
-- real: token_bucket.lua
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', tostring(now))
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity * 1000 / rate) + 1000)
local reset = math.ceil((capacity - tokens) * 1000 / rate)
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens), retry, reset}
advantages: Slow rates pe bhi exact refill
disadvantages: Float precision ke bahut lambe periods pe tiny drift
cost > capacity case ka special handling nahi
common_mistakes: Integer tokens store karna
TTL fixed (jaise 1 hour) rakhna -- memory waste ya early deletion
follow_up_questions: What if cost is larger than capacity?
Why write state even on denial?
How would GCRA store this in a single number?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Hash (2 fields) vs GCRA ki single TAT value: hash readable hai, GCRA compact. Project ne readability choose ki.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis restart pe state lost -> bucket full -> client ko fresh burst. Soft state ke roop mein accepted (FAILURE_SCENARIOS #4).
advanced.alternatives: GCRA (theoretical arrival time) jo ek timestamp store karta hai; ya fixed-point integer arithmetic (milli-tokens) taaki floats na hon.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Lakhon keys pe hash overhead matter karta hai; Redis small hashes ko listpack encoding mein rakhta hai, toh 2-field hash sasta hai. 100x pe GCRA ka single string aur sasta.
advanced.production_improvements: cost > capacity validation add karo (policy/route level), aur integer milli-tokens consider karo agar precision audit chahiye.

question: How does RedisRateLimiter load and call the scripts (EVALSHA, NOSCRIPT)?
answer_hinglish:
`RedisRateLimiter.__init__` har `Algorithm` ke liye `redis.register_script(_load(alg.value))` call karta hai. `_load` `lua/<name>.lua` file padhta hai. `register_script` ek `Script` object deta hai jo script ka SHA1 locally compute karta hai.

Jab hum `await script(keys=[...], args=[...])` call karte hain, redis-py `EVALSHA <sha1>` bhejta hai -- poora script text nahi, sirf 40-char hash. Isse har request pe network pe kam bytes jaate hain aur Redis ko script dobara parse nahi karni padti.

Agar Redis ke script cache mein woh SHA nahi hai (Redis restart, failover, `SCRIPT FLUSH`), toh Redis `NOSCRIPT` error deta hai. redis-py ka `Script.__call__` yeh error pakad ke script ko load karke (EVAL/SCRIPT LOAD) dobara chalata hai -- transparently. Test `test_survives_script_cache_flush` exactly yeh karta hai: ek call, `redis.script_flush()`, phir doosri call -- dono allowed.

Phir `check` result `allowed, remaining, retry_ms, reset_ms` unpack karke `Decision` dataclass banata hai. Errors: `ConnectionError`, `TimeoutError`, `OSError` aur baaki `RedisError` (jaise READONLY replica ya OOM) sab `BackendUnavailable` mein convert hote hain, taaki service layer policy ke fail_mode ke hisaab se decide kare.
why_needed: Har request pe poora script bhejna wasteful hai; NOSCRIPT handling na ho toh Redis restart ke baad saare checks fail.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein poori recipe har baar bolne ke bajaye dish ka number bolo; agar naya chef number nahi jaanta toh ek baar recipe de do.
how_it_works: EVALSHA sha numkeys keys... args...; Redis script cache sha -> compiled function. Cache volatile hai (restart pe khali).
in_this_project: `limiter/redis_limiter.py::RedisRateLimiter.check` aur `__init__`; comment: "register_script uses EVALSHA ... falls back to EVAL on NOSCRIPT".
advantages: Ek jagah se saare scripts manage
disadvantages: Pehli call pe extra round-trip (NOSCRIPT + load)
Pipeline ke andar NOSCRIPT handling tricky
common_mistakes: SHA ko hardcode karna aur restart pe fail hona
Har request pe EVAL with full text
follow_up_questions: What is Redis Functions (Redis 7) and how is it different?
How does NOSCRIPT behave inside a pipeline?
Why map RedisError to BackendUnavailable?

question: How is the Redis key for a rate limit counter built?
answer_hinglish:
Key do layers mein banti hai. Service layer `_identity_key` identity key banata hai: scope prefix + id, jaise `ip:1.2.3.4`, `user:alice`, `api_key:3f9a...`. Agar scope ka id None hai (anonymous user hitting user-scoped policy) toh `anon-ip:1.2.3.4`.

Phir limiter layer `build_key(policy, key)` final key banata hai: `f"{KEY_PREFIX}:{policy.name}:{{{key}}}"` -- matlab `rl:user_plan:{ip:1.2.3.4}`. Python f-string mein `{{` aur `}}` literal braces hain, toh identity curly braces mein aati hai.

Har part ka reason: `rl:` prefix namespace -- doosre apps ki keys se collision nahi, aur `SCAN MATCH rl:*` se debugging. Policy name -- ek identity ke alag policies ke counters alag. Scope prefix -- ip "alice" aur user "alice" collide nahi karte. Curly braces -- Redis Cluster hash tag: cluster sirf `{}` ke andar ke part ko hash karta hai, toh ek identity ki saari keys same slot pe jaati hain.

Fixed window aur sliding counter is base key ke aage `:window_start` lagate hain (jaise `rl:user_plan:{ip:1.2.3.4}:1700000040000`), aur sliding counter ek hi script mein current aur previous dono keys touch karta hai -- hash tag ki wajah se dono same slot pe hain. Test mein key `rl:test:{u1}:<T0>` directly padhi jati hai.
why_needed: Key design hi data model hai; galat key = collisions, cluster errors, ya debugging nightmare.
real_world_analogy: Courier ka address: city (rl), building (policy), flat (identity), aur pin code (hash tag) jo decide karta hai kaunsa post office deliver karega.
how_it_works: Key = prefix:policy:{scope:id}[:window_start]. Cluster slot = CRC16(hash tag) mod 16384.
in_this_project: `redis_limiter.py::build_key`, `rate_limit_service.py::_identity_key`, `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` key table.
disadvantages: Lambi keys = thodi zyada memory
IPv6 addresses keys ko aur lamba banate hain
common_mistakes: Hash tag mein policy name daalna (sab identities ek slot pe -- hot shard)
Scope prefix bhool jana
follow_up_questions: What would happen if the hash tag were the policy name?
Would you hash the identity to shorten keys?
How do you find all keys of one user?
